 UN Loss and Damage Fund provisionally approves $21.6 million for flood-hit Nepal
 Simrin Sirur 
 26 Oct 2026 
 Global Climate Finance 
 Comments 
 Share article 
 Share this article
 If you liked this story, share it with other people.

 Page link 
 Nepal, which suffered a catastrophic debris flow and flash flood on August 26, is slated to receive $21.6 million from the United Nations’ Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD).
 The decision to “provisionally” release the funds was finalised during an “extraordinary meeting” convened by the Fund’s board on October 22. Nepal will still need to apply for this funding, and the Board will consider the request at its next meeting, the tenth FRLD Board meeting, this December.
 “Following Nepal’s formal letter on August 31, 2026 requesting support from the Fund, the FRLD Board commenced to assess available options. Backed by strong solidarity from the whole Board, intensive consultations were held throughout September and October, culminating in today’s extraordinary Board meeting, in accordance with the Board’s Rules of Procedure,” an FRLD press statement said .
 The FRLD was constituted in 2023 with the specific purpose of providing rapid financial support to developing countries struggling with the economic and non-economic losses and damages associated with climate-driven extreme weather events.
 The demand by developing countries for a funding facility for losses and damages had been simmering at the climate Conference of Parties (COP) meetings for decades. The decision to provisionally release funding to Nepal comes ahead of the COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled to take place from November 9 to November 20.
 Climate change was “a destabilising factor” in the Nepal flash flood, according to a report by the World Weather Attribution. The trigger was the rapid collapse of a 2-square-kilometre wall of rock and glacier ice, but “warming and permafrost degradation likely weakened the source rock wall by increasing bedrock temperatures and thawing ice within fractures,” said the WWA which conducts rapid attribution studies to quantify how climate change influences the intensity and likelihood of an extreme weather event. 
 About 1,300 people – including hundreds of Indian pilgrims – died in the Nepal floods. Damages were estimated to be up to $2.69 billion. The Nepal government told the FRLD that the initial cost of recovery and reconstruction would cost $4.71 billion.
 “The Loss and Damage Fund took a historic first step by responding to Nepal, but this cannot be a one-off,” said Harjeet Singh, Global Convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign, in a statement. “No country should have to endure a catastrophe and wait seven weeks, through historic letters and relentless pressure, just to unlock the Fund’s first-ever emergency meeting. We must set up a permanent rapid-response system that moves support in days, not months.”
